<reason>Both sides were skilled, but A answered more of the decisive pressures directly. B's central weapon was the dilemma: funding either means conditions (boardroom colonialism) or unconditional transfer (mere aid, not obligation). A neutralized it with a mechanism seeded in the opening and sharpened across rounds — an irrevocable, recipient-directed endowment that is neither conditional control nor revocable charity. B's rejoinder ("patronage with better manners," "a mood, not a mechanism") asserted incoherence rather than demonstrating it, and B never engaged A's point that a one-time capitalized endowment also answers the "conservation is perpetual spending" objection. A cleanly defeated the insult charge ("you can care, so we owe the means"), gave compliant, direct A1/A2 answers, and addressed B's best late point (who certifies capacity) by denying London any certifying role. B's strongest surviving material was the scope objection — that stripped-revenue damages is a general colonial claim, not an artifact-attached debt — which A softened but never fully resolved. B was more rhetorically crystallized and the clipped opening was a minor cost. On balance, A held the proposition with a coherent account of obligation without control; B's counterattacks increasingly relied on reasserted framing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The dilemma exchange in Rebuttal 2: B argued that obligation-without-control is incoherent and that PRO's finish line lets the former taker certify the recipient's "adequacy." A's polluter-endowment analogy (a finite, one-time transfer whose interest funds ongoing care) plus the distinction between revocable aid and a non-revocable duty gave the most substantive escape of the debate, and A's closing ("a duty you cannot revoke is not a gift you cannot refuse") landed the cleaner final word on that clash.</best_rebuttal>
